Splitting the Lunch Budget

Split a 404040 lunch budget between two foods. The money constraint is one line: p1x1+p2x2=mp_1 x_1 + p_2 x_2 = mp1​x1​+p2​x2​=m. The best combo is where the last won buys the same happiness everywhere — raise a price and watch that point slide.

p1x1+p2x2=mp_1 x_1 + p_2 x_2 = mp1​x1​+p2​x2​=m
MU1p1=MU2p2\frac{MU_1}{p_1} = \frac{MU_2}{p_2}p1​MU1​​=p2​MU2​​

Examples & Exercises

Lunch budget m=40m = 40m=40, food 1 costs p1=4p_1 = 4p1​=4, food 2 costs p2=8p_2 = 8p2​=8. The budget equation is p1x1+p2x2=mp_1 x_1 + p_2 x_2 = mp1​x1​+p2​x2​=m — liking both, how should the budget be split?

Show proof
  1. Going all-in on one food unbalances the happiness of the last won. Balance comes when the last won buys the same happiness either way.
  2. That point splits the budget exactly in half: 202020 worth of food 1 (555 items) and 202020 worth of food 2 (2.52.52.5 items). That is why the two readout lines show the same number.

Food 1's price halves from 444 to 222. How many of each food get bought now?

Show proof
  1. Surprisingly, food 2 stays at 2.52.52.5 items. The split-in-half rule holds regardless of prices.
  2. Food 1: 202020 worth at 222 each is 101010 items — you buy more of the cheaper food, but the other food's share is untouched. That is the signature of this preference.
